legend: Let's call a sequence b1,b2,b3…,bk−1,bk%%ZSMJ0%% almost increasing if min(b1,b2)≤min(b2,b3)≤⋯≤min(bk−1,bk).%%ZSMJ1%% In particular, any sequence with no more than two elements is almost increasing.
You are given a sequence of integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ2%%. Calculate the length of its longest almost increasing subsequence.
You'll be given t%%ZSMJ3%% test cases. Solve each test case independently.
Reminder: a subsequence is a sequence that can be derived from another sequence by deleting some elements without changing the order of the remaining elements.
input: The first line contains a single integer t%%ZSMJ4%% (1≤t≤1000%%ZSMJ5%%) — the number of independent test cases.
The first line of each test case contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ6%% (2≤n≤5⋅105%%ZSMJ7%%) — the length of the sequence a%%ZSMJ8%%.
The second line of each test case contains n%%ZSMJ9%% integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ10%% (1≤ai≤n%%ZSMJ11%%) — the sequence itself.
It's guaranteed that the total sum of n%%ZSMJ12%% over all test cases doesn't exceed 5⋅105%%ZSMJ13%%.
output: For each test case, print one integer — the length of the longest almost increasing subsequence.
note: In the first test case, one of the optimal answers is subsequence 1,2,7,2,2,3%%ZSMJ14%%.
In the second and third test cases, the whole sequence a%%ZSMJ15%% is already almost increasing.
